title: Cambodian Fish Amok (Amok Trey) in Banana-Leaf Cups
dek: Firm white fish steams in a silky lemongrass, turmeric and coconut custard, with practical folded-leaf cups and a ramekin fallback for home kitchens.
image_alt: Three orange-gold Cambodian fish amok custards in square banana-leaf cups, topped with white coconut cream, red chile strips and green herbs
ingredients: 8 frozen or fresh banana-leaf squares, each 8 inches, thawed if frozen, plus extra in case of tears
1 1/2 pounds (680 g) skinless firm white fish fillets, such as cod, haddock or catfish, cut into 1-inch pieces and patted dry
1 can (13.5 ounces/400 ml) full-fat coconut milk, refrigerated overnight without shaking
2 large eggs
1 tablespoon fish sauce, plus more to taste
2 teaspoons palm sugar or light brown sugar
1 teaspoon fine sea salt, divided
1 teaspoon rice flour or cornstarch
1 small red chile, seeded and cut into thin lengthwise strips
8 small Thai basil leaves or cilantro sprigs
Hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving (optional)
2 tender inner lemongrass stalk sections, bottom 4 inches only, very thinly sliced (about 3 tablespoons)
2 medium shallots, roughly chopped
4 garlic cloves, smashed
1 tablespoon peeled and minced fresh galangal, or 2 teaspoons peeled fresh ginger
2 makrut lime leaves, center ribs removed and leaves finely sliced, plus 1 leaf for garnish
1 fresh red bird's-eye chile, stemmed, or 1/2 teaspoon red-pepper flakes
1 teaspoon peeled and grated fresh turmeric, or 3/4 teaspoon ground turmeric
1 teaspoon shrimp paste (optional but traditional in character)
2 tablespoons neutral oil, such as avocado or grapeseed

instructions.name: Soften and sanitize the banana leaves
instructions.text: Rinse both sides of the banana-leaf squares and wipe them dry. Pass each square 4 to 6 inches above a medium gas flame for 5 to 8 seconds per side, or lay it in a dry skillet over medium heat for 10 to 15 seconds per side, just until glossy and flexible. Do not char it. Wipe again with a clean damp towel and keep covered so the leaves do not become brittle.

instructions.name: Fold four leak-resistant cups
instructions.text: Stack two softened squares with their grain running in opposite directions. Center a 4-inch ramekin on top, lift the leaves around it and make four overlapping pleats to form a 4-inch-wide cup about 2 inches deep. Secure each corner through the outer edge with a wooden toothpick, never through the cup base. Remove the ramekin and repeat to make four double-layer cups. Set them in a steamer basket or shallow heatproof pan where they stand level.

instructions.name: Pound a fine kroeung-style paste
instructions.text: Put the lemongrass, shallots, garlic, galangal, 2 sliced makrut lime leaves, bird's-eye chile, turmeric, shrimp paste if using and oil in a small food processor. Process for 60 to 90 seconds, stopping twice to scrape the bowl, until the mixture is a moist, finely textured paste with no hard lemongrass rings. Add 1 teaspoon water only if the blades cannot catch.

instructions.name: Cook the aromatics without browning
instructions.text: Scrape the paste into a small skillet and cook over medium-low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until intensely fragrant and slightly thickened but not browned. Cool for 5 minutes. This short cook softens the aromatics so the finished custard is smooth rather than fibrous.

instructions.name: Separate the coconut cream topping
instructions.text: Open the chilled coconut milk without shaking. Spoon 1/3 cup of the thick cream from the top into a small saucepan; whisk in the rice flour and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Measure 3/4 cup of the remaining coconut milk for the custard, stirring the can first if needed. Reserve any extra for another use.

instructions.name: Coat the fish in the coconut custard
instructions.text: Whisk the eggs, 3/4 cup coconut milk, cooked aromatic paste, fish sauce, palm sugar and remaining 3/4 teaspoon salt in a medium bowl until uniform. Fold in the dry fish pieces and stand for 10 minutes while the steamer heats. The mixture should coat the fish rather than look watery; if the fish released liquid, lift it into a clean bowl before adding the custard.

instructions.name: Heat the steamer before filling
instructions.text: Bring 1 1/2 inches of water to a steady simmer in a wide covered pot or wok fitted with a rack or steamer basket. The water must stay below the basket. Wrap the lid in a clean kitchen towel and tie the ends above the lid, away from the burner, so condensation cannot drip into the custards.

instructions.name: Fill and steam gently
instructions.text: Divide the fish and custard evenly among the four cups, keeping a 1/2-inch headspace. Set the cups in the hot steamer without letting them touch the water. Cover and steam over medium heat for 18 minutes; keep the water at a steady simmer, not a violent boil. Rotate the basket carefully, then steam 4 to 8 minutes longer, until the centers are softly set and a thin-probe thermometer inserted into the thickest fish-and-custard area reads at least 160°F.

instructions.name: Thicken the coconut finish
instructions.text: While the amok steams, set the saucepan of coconut cream over medium-low heat. Whisk for 2 to 3 minutes, until it just simmers and lightly coats the whisk. Remove from the heat; it should be spoonable, not stiff. If it thickens too much, whisk in 1 teaspoon water.

instructions.name: Garnish to match the finished dish
instructions.text: Rest the cooked cups in the open steamer for 3 minutes. Spoon a stripe of thickened white coconut cream over each orange-gold custard, then add red chile strips, very thinly sliced makrut lime leaf and two basil leaves or a small cilantro sprig. Remove or point out the securing toothpicks before serving with hot jasmine rice, if desired.

why_it_works: Finely processing and briefly cooking the lemongrass-heavy paste releases its aromatic oils while taming the tough fibers before they enter the delicate custard.
Patting the fish dry and using full-fat coconut milk keeps the egg-to-liquid ratio controlled, so the amok sets softly instead of weeping.
Double-layered banana leaves with opposing grain directions resist small tears and hold the custard upright while contributing a subtle leafy aroma.
A steady simmer and a towel-wrapped lid prevent aggressive bubbles and condensation from pitting or diluting the custard surface.
The 160°F center target accounts for the egg custard as well as the fish, whose separate FDA minimum is 145°F.
Rice flour gives the coconut topping enough body to remain visibly white on the hot orange-gold custard, matching the traditional-style presentation without turning gluey.
swaps: Use haddock, catfish, halibut or tilapia in place of cod; choose thick, firm fillets and cut them uniformly. Avoid very oily fish or delicate sole, which can overwhelm or fall apart in the custard.
If banana leaves are unavailable, lightly oil four 6-ounce ramekins and set them on the steamer rack. The flavor will be less leafy, but the custard timing and safe-temperature test remain the same.

Fresh ginger can replace galangal, and lime zest can replace makrut lime leaf in the custard. Both are useful home-kitchen substitutions, but their flavors are not identical to the Cambodian aromatic profile.
For a shellfish-free version, omit the shrimp paste and add 1 additional teaspoon fish sauce. For a fully seafood-free version, this is not the right recipe; the fish is central to amok trey.
Ground turmeric works well in the paste. Fresh turmeric gives a brighter aroma but stains hands and equipment, so wear gloves and use a nonporous board.
storage: Remove garnishes, cool the cups promptly and refrigerate covered at 40°F or below within 2 hours. Eat within 2 days. Reheat in a covered steamer over gently simmering water for 8 to 10 minutes, or cover loosely and microwave at 50% power in 45-second intervals, until the center reaches 165°F. The egg-coconut custard can become grainy after freezing, so freezing is not recommended. Discard banana-leaf cups after serving.
notes: Cultural and naming note: regional tourism guidance describes amok trey as a Khmer steamed fish curry cake or turmeric-coconut fish custard, commonly cooked in banana leaf. This home-kitchen version preserves the defining fish, kroeung-style aromatic paste, coconut-and-egg custard, banana-leaf vessel and steaming method while naming substitutions honestly.

Photo-match record: the licensed photograph is explicitly identified by its creator as three servings of amok trey. It visibly shows orange-gold steamed custard in square banana-leaf cups with white coconut cream, thin red chile strips and green herbs; every major visible element appears in the title, ingredients, method and alt text.

Banana-leaf cup sizing guide — 8-inch double squares around a 4-inch ramekin make a 4-inch cup for one quarter of this recipe; 7-inch squares make a narrower, taller cup that may need 3 to 5 extra steaming minutes; 9-inch squares are easier for beginners but require a wider steamer. Always keep a 1/2-inch headspace and secure only the outer walls.

Steamer conversion guide — bamboo basket over a wok: 22 to 26 minutes with the best condensation control; metal basket in a stockpot: 24 to 28 minutes with the lid wrapped; ramekins on a rack: 25 to 30 minutes because ceramic heats more slowly. Time is a guide only; all versions must reach 160°F in the center.

Custard diagnostic — watery before steaming: the fish was not dried or the coconut milk was too thin; bubbles and holes: the water boiled too hard; unset after 28 minutes: cups are crowded or the steamer lost heat; rubbery edge: the cups steamed too long. Adjust the simmer first and use temperature, not color, to call doneness.

Food-safety note: FDA guidance lists 145°F for fin fish and 160°F for egg dishes. Because amok is an egg-bound fish custard, this recipe uses the more protective 160°F center target; leftovers should be reheated to 165°F.

faqs.q: Can I make fish amok without banana leaves?
faqs.a: Yes. Lightly oil four 6-ounce heatproof ramekins, fill them with the same 1/2-inch headspace and steam for about 25 to 30 minutes. Start checking at 24 minutes and require 160°F in the center. You will lose the leaf aroma and traditional-style presentation, but the fish custard will still set correctly.

faqs.q: Why did my amok turn watery instead of custardy?
faqs.a: The usual causes are wet fish, thin coconut beverage instead of canned full-fat coconut milk, or condensation dripping from the lid. Pat the fish very dry, measure only 3/4 cup coconut milk into the two eggs, wrap the lid and keep the water at a steady simmer. Let the cups rest 3 minutes so the custard finishes settling.

faqs.q: Is fish amok very spicy, and can I make it mild?
faqs.a: It should be aromatic and warm rather than aggressively hot. For a mild version, omit the bird's-eye chile from the paste and use the red garnish chile only on servings that want it. Do not remove the lemongrass, turmeric, galangal and makrut lime leaf; those aromatics, not chile heat, define the fragrant profile.
